title: Embedding router: token-aware admission & soft-tenant budgets
creator: Ava Chen
description:
Problem: production embedding endpoints are sensitive to bursty tenant behaviour. Small tenants triggering many short requests can increase request-per-second (RPS) while producing tiny batches, which hurts GPU utilization and raises token cost. Current autoscaler reacts to queue length and GPU utilization but lacks tenant-aware admission, token-aware batching signals, and graceful fallback when capacity is constrained.

Goal: ship an admission controller in the embedding router that is token-size aware and enforces soft per-tenant concurrency budgets (headroom tokens) combined with a burstable warm-pool strategy. This should reduce tail latency under multi-tenant contention, improve average tokens-per-batch on GPUs, and provide predictable cost behavior for customers. The feature should be observable (per-tenant metrics), compatible with rate limits at API gateway layer, and have a staged rollout with canary traffic and automatic fallback to degraded embedding variants (sparse/quantized) when required.
acceptance_criteria: Router implements token-aware admission: requests supply estimated token count and router uses that to compute admission cost
Soft per-tenant budget enforces headroom tokens with decay-based refill; tenant can burst above budget but will be probabilistically admitted when over budget
Observed median embedding latency under 95th percentile tail reduces by >= 15% for mixed-tenant load in staging compared to baseline
GPU tokens-per-batch increases by >= 25% on representative workload trace in performance lab
Metrics emitted: tenant_headroom_available, tenant_overbudget_rate, router_admit_latency, batch_tokens, batch_size; all visible in Grafana dashboard
End-to-end tests and chaos test demonstrating graceful fallback to quantized/sparse model variant when warm-pool exhausted
Runbook updated with operational playbook and cost impact estimation
proposed_solution:
1) Extend embedding request envelope so clients include token_estimate (optional). If absent, router uses a conservative heuristic.
2) Admission controller computes per-request cost = token_estimate * model_cost_weight(model_family). Maintain per-tenant soft_budget (headroom) with a leaky-bucket refill and integer headroom tokens.
3) When a tenant is over budget, apply probabilistic admission where admission probability p = exp(-alpha * overage_tokens / headroom). p tuned by experiment. Over-budget requests may be queued or rejected with a 429-like response + Retry-After.
4) Integrate with batching pipeline: prefer grouping admitted requests to maximize batch token utilization while respecting max_batch_size and latency SLO. Use a two-tier queue (hot vs warm) where hot queue is for requests within headroom; warm queue drains via warm-pool workers that can be pre-warmed.
5) Warm-pool: maintain a small number of hot workers per region that keep KV cache primed (configurable). Warm-pool scale rules based on sustained token throughput, not request count.
6) Autoscaler changes: feed token-based throughput metric (tokens/s) to autoscaler in addition to GPU utilization to drive more stable scale events.
7) Observability: expose per-tenant metrics, sampled request traces, and capacity-simulator outputs used by planner.
8) Fallback path: when capacity constrained, router can route to lower-cost embedding variant (e.g., 8-bit quantized or sparse) with gradual degradation labels and customer-facing guidance.
tradeoffs_and_risks:
- Complexity: introduces per-tenant state and probabilistic admission; operational burden for SREs.
- Fairness tuning: improperly tuned alpha or headroom values may starve small tenants or allow noisy tenants to consume disproportionate GPU tokens.
- Client dependency: token_estimate is optional; router heuristics may mis-estimate leading to suboptimal admission.
- Observability overhead: per-tenant metrics at high cardinality could increase metric ingestion costs; plan to sample or use cardinality controls.
- Fallback quality: quantized/sparse variants may degrade downstream relevance; need QA and customer communication.
- Rollout risk: warm-pool mis-sizing could increase costs if left too large; require automated budget guardrails.
implementation_tasks: Router: request schema extension + heuristic estimator (ENG)
Admission controller: per-tenant budget store (in-memory + persisted checkpoint) (ENG)
Batching change: two-tier queue and token-aware batch builder (ENG)
Warm-pool: worker lifecycle + priming logic + autoscale hook (ENG)
Autoscaler: accept tokens/s metric and new scaling policy (ENG)
Observability: metrics, dashboards, and SLO checks (ENG/Infra)
End-to-end tests: perf lab replay + chaos test + regression suite (QA)
Docs: API changelog, Console configuration UI spec, Runbook (PM/Docs)
rollout_plan:
Phase 1 (staging): feature flag on; token_estimate optional; run with 10% of staging tenant traffic. Validate metrics and batch composition.
Phase 2 (canary): 2 production tenants opt-in (low-risk customers) for 1 week with close SRE monitoring. Adjust headroom and alpha.
Phase 3 (regional ramp): enable in US-west for 20% traffic, runbook execute rehearsals.
Phase 4 (global): enable by default with conservative headroom and enable opt-out per-tenant.
Rollback: feature-flag off, auto-warmpool scale-down script, and immediate routing to legacy admission path.
Communication: release notes, customer-facing KB on embedding degradation and recommended client-side token_estimate usage.
testing_plan:
- Synthetic perf-lab trace replay comparing baseline vs admission-controller: measure tokens-per-batch and latency percentiles.
- Integration test: simulate 1k tenants with Zipf distribution of QPS to verify headroom fairness and admission equilibria.
- Chaos: kill warm-pool workers to ensure graceful fallback and verify runbook steps.
- E2E canary with opt-in tenants: monitor business metrics for potential regression in retrieval/semantic-search quality.
- Load test: exercise autoscaler with tokens/s metric and validate no oscillation over 10-minute window.
open_questions: Default headroom sizing: should it be proportional to tenant historical tokens/s or fixed per-org tier?
Should over-budget rejection return HTTP 429 or a 200 with degraded-embedding warning to preserve client UX?
What cardinality controls do we need for tenant metrics to avoid Prometheus explosion?
How to best communicate degraded embedding fallback to customers and permit opt-out?
